---
title: "Unit 3: Spatial Data Sources and Quality"
---

Every dataset has a source, a method, and limits. This unit is about where spatial data come from and how far to trust them. It starts with the largest source of free data about people and places in the United States, the census, and how to read its estimates honestly, then tours the other federal agencies whose free imagery, land cover, elevation, water, and hazard data underlie most GIS work in the country. It turns to data made by volunteers, in OpenStreetMap, and the elements of data quality, then to uncertainty: how to measure it, where it enters, and how to show it on a map. It ends with one of the most widely used data sets of all, the digital elevation model, and the tools that turn elevation into slope, hillshade, aspect, and viewsheds. By the end of the unit you can find, judge, and document spatial data in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.

## Chapter 9: [Census Data](../chapters/census-data.qmd)

The U.S. Census Bureau decides how many members of Congress each state gets and where trillions of federal dollars go. This chapter separates authoritative from asserted data and describes the decennial census, the American Community Survey, and the Economic Census. It explains the hierarchy of census geography, from states to blocks, and the GEOIDs that identify each area. It shows how to choose between decennial, ACS 1-year, and ACS 5-year data, how to read a margin of error, and how to join a census table to its boundaries in ArcGIS Pro.

## Chapter 10: [Federal Spatial Data Sets](../chapters/federal-data.qmd)

Beyond the census, U.S. federal agencies publish free, nationally consistent data for almost every GIS project. This chapter tours the ones used most: NAIP aerial photography, the National Land Cover Database, Landsat, MODIS, and NASA Earthdata, the 3D Elevation Program, the National Hydrography Dataset and its nested watersheds, FEMA's flood maps and National Risk Index, and EPA's water quality tools. For each it covers who makes it, what it measures, its resolution and update cycle, and where to download it, and it ends with how to choose between them and how to read, record, and cite federal data.

## Chapter 11: [OpenStreetMap and Data Quality](../chapters/osm-data-quality.qmd)

What makes geographic data good enough to use? This chapter defines spatial data quality by its seven elements, from lineage to completeness, then looks at volunteered geographic information, Big Data, and the FAIR principles. It explains how OpenStreetMap works, from its license to its nodes, ways, and tags, and how its quality is measured against authoritative data and from its own history. It ends with crisis mapping, from Haiti in 2010 to the 2015 Nepal earthquake, where thousands of new volunteers mapped a country in weeks.

## Chapter 12: [Uncertainty in Geospatial Data](../chapters/uncertainty.qmd)

Every map is uncertain. This chapter separates uncertainty from error, revisits the seven elements of data quality with examples, and shows how to measure positional accuracy with RMSE and accuracy standards. It traces how uncertainty enters at every stage from collection to use, explains Type 1 and Type 2 errors in map reading, and shows how crispness, transparency, saturation, and added symbols put uncertainty on the map.

[Chapter 12 quiz](../chapters/uncertainty-quiz.qmd)
:::

## Chapter 13: [Digital Elevation Models](../chapters/digital-elevation-models.qmd)

Elevation is the most widely used raster of all. This chapter traces elevation mapping from hill drawings and contour lines to digital elevation models, explains how lidar and radar collect elevation and how DEMs, DTMs, and DSMs differ, and shows how to download a DEM from The National Map and check it for problems. Using Linville Gorge, it works through slope (Horn's and Fleming and Hoffer's methods), hillshade, aspect, line of sight, and viewshed.
